slides.title: What is Material Science?
text: What is Material Science?
• Interdisciplinary field studying the properties, structure,
and processing of materials (metals, ceramics, polymers, etc.)
• Key challenges include designing new materials with targeted properties
(for energy, electronics, etc.) and scaling up from lab to industry
• Applications to semiconductors, batteries, biomaterials, and more

slides.title: Key Challenges in Materials Discovery
text: Key Challenges in Materials Discovery
• Key challenges:
• Vast design space: Millions of potential compounds,
but only a fraction have been synthesized.
• Traditional trial-and-error synthesis is slow and costly.
• Simulations (e.g. DFT) for crystal structures are
accurate but time-consuming.
• Inverse design problem: Use AI to go from
desired property to a material that exhibits it.

slides.title: Types of Materials
text: Types of Materials
• Metals (iron, copper): good electrical conductors,
ductile, often crystalline.
• Ceramics (alumina, silicon carbide): inorganic
compounds, brittle but withstand high temperatures.
• Polymers (plastics like PE, PTFE): long-chain
organic molecules, lightweight and flexible.
• Composites: combinations of materials

slides.title: Types of Material Properties
text: Types of Material Properties
• Classification by electronic properties:
• Conductors (e.g., metals):
Have free electrons that allow easy charge flow. No band gap.
• Insulators (e.g., ceramics, polymers):
No free carriers under normal conditions. Large band gap.
• Semiconductors (in between):
Conductivity can be tuned by doping or temperature. Moderate band gap.
• Band gap is the energy difference (in electronvolts, eV) between:
• The top of the valence band (highest energy electrons bound to atoms)
• The bottom of the conduction band (lowest energy electrons that can move freely)
• Conceptually similar to HOMO-LUMO gap for molecules (non-materials)

slides.title: Types of Material Properties
text: Types of Material Properties
• Classification by optical properties
• Transparency:
• Occurs when a material does not absorb visible light.
• Requires a wide band gap, so photons pass through without excitation (e.g., glass, quartz).
• Luminescence:
• Emission of light from a material after absorbing energy.
• Can arise from electron-hole recombination (photoluminescence),
defects (fluorescence), or dopants (phosphors in LEDs).

slides.title: Types of Material Properties                                              Electrons = real particles that move and
text: Types of Material Properties                                              Electrons = real particles that move and
carry charge.
Phonons = waves of atomic motion,
• Classification by thermal properties                                    quantized as particles of vibration.
• Thermal conductors:
• Heat transported via free electrons (metals) or phonons (diamond).
• Strong atomic bonds and high atomic density enhance conductivity.
• Thermal insulators:
• Poor phonon or electron transport.
• Often disordered, porous, or low-density structures.

slides.title: Types of Material Properties
text: Types of Material Properties
• Classification by magnetic properties
• Diamagnetic: Weak repulsion to magnetic fields.
• Paramagnetic: Materials with unpaired electrons
align weakly with external fields.
• Ferromagnetic: Strong magnetic ordering; domains
align spontaneously.
• Antiferromagnetic / ferrimagnetic: Opposing spin
alignments reduce or partially cancel net
magnetization (e.g., MnO, Fe₃O₄).

slides.title: Types of Material Properties
text: Types of Material Properties
• Hardness: Resistance to deformation or scratching
• Elasticity: Ability to return to original shape after stress
• Plasticity: Permanent deformation under stress;
common in metals due to dislocation motion.
• Toughness: Resistance to fracture (balance between strength and ductility).
Brittle materials (e.g., ceramics) fracture easily;

slides.title: Unit Cells and Lattices
text: Unit Cells and Lattices
• Bravais lattice: distinct lattice types (14 in
3D) describing all possible periodic
arrangements of points.
• These include primitive and centered lattices for
each crystal system
• Each lattice type is associated with a set of
translations that leaves the crystal invariant.
• NOT associated with a particular group!

slides.title: Symmetry in Crystal Structures
text: Symmetry in Crystal Structures
• Crystals exhibit symmetry operations:
• translations, rotations, reflections, inversion that map the
crystal onto itself.
• Translational symmetry:
• the repeating lattice means a translation by one unit cell
leaves the crystal unchanged
• Point symmetry:
• Rotations or inversions about lattice points,
e.g., a cube has 90° rotational axes and mirror planes.               Allows additional
translation
• Combination of point symmetries with translations gives the
full space group symmetry
Allows 6-fold rotation

slides.title: Space Group Symmetry
text: Space Group Symmetry
• Space groups (230 distinct groups in 3D) which enumerate all combinations of rotations,
mirrors, glide planes, screw axes with translations that a crystal can have.
• Obtained from removing duplicates in 14x32 combinations.
2D space groups

slides.title: Wyckoff Positions
text: Wyckoff Positions
• Wyckoff positions: within a space group, these are sets of points in the unit cell that are
equivalent under symmetry. Atoms in a crystal occupy Wyckoff positions.
• High-symmetry positions often lead to more stable structures,
many known materials have atoms on special symmetric sites

slides.title: Crystal Property Prediction
text: Crystal Property Prediction
• Formation energy and stability: Geometric deep learning (CGCNN, MEGNet, etc.) can
predict formation energies of crystals with high accuracy.
• Formation energy is the energy required to form a compound from
its constituent elements in their standard states
• Allows rapid screening of millions of hypothetical structures for
thermodynamic stability (negative formation energy).

slides.title: Crystal Property Prediction
text: Crystal Property Prediction
• Band gap prediction: Models have been trained to predict band gaps.
• Enabling quick identification of candidate semiconductors
• Band gap is the energy difference (in electronvolts, eV) between:
• The top of the valence band (highest energy electrons bound to atoms)
• The bottom of the conduction band (lowest energy electrons that can move freely)

slides.title: Crystal Structure Prediction
text: Crystal Structure Prediction
• Traditional materials discovery predicts properties of a given
structure, while inverse design asks: what structure yields a
desired property?
• Crystal Structure Prediction (CSP) methods (e.g., USPEX,
random search) tackle this by finding low-energy structures for
a given composition but are computationally expensive.
• ML-based CSP uses generative models to learn and sample
from the distribution of stable structures, enabling exploration
of many candidates or even novel compositions.
• ML can also be embedded in an active learning loop: propose
→ evaluate → refine, accelerating inverse design by focusing
on structures with promising properties.

slides.title: DiffCSP
text: DiffCSP
• DiffCSP is a diffusion model to generate crystal structure from compositions.
• Equivariant to rotations and translations.
• Invariant to periodic transformations.

slides.title: DiffCSP++: Space Group Constraints
text: DiffCSP++: Space Group Constraints
• DiffCSP++ allows explicit conditioning on space group symmetry for structure generation.
• First sample a lattice, then assign atoms to Wyckoff positions
(including which Wyckoff sites are occupied and by what element).
• Then sample any displacements within those sites (constrained by symmetry).
Drastically improves performance.

slides.title: SymmCD – Symmetry-Preserving Diffusion
text: SymmCD – Symmetry-Preserving Diffusion
• SymmCD also generates crystal structures conditioned on symmetry,
but keeps the representation size small.
• Separates the crystal into asymmetric unit (minimal atom set)
and space group operations (applied post-generation).

slides.title: Crystal Generative Models
text: Crystal Generative Models
• Generating the crystal composition along with 3D coordinates.
• These models often have capability of crystal structure prediction through conditioning.
• The pipeline for generative design often is:
• generate candidate materials (with a generative model)
• predict their properties (with a fast ML model)
• filter or optimize
• possibly feedback to generator.

slides.title: Crystal Diffusion VAE (CDVAE)
text: Crystal Diffusion VAE (CDVAE)
• In CDVAE, the encoder maps a crystal structure to a latent vector, and the decoder
attempts to reconstruct the structure by a diffusion process.

slides.title: CrystalLLM
text: CrystalLLM
• Tokenize crystallographic CIF files and train autoregressive transformer .
• At generation time, you prompt it with a desired composition,
and it writes out a plausible crystal structure as a CIF file

slides.title: Finetuning Existing LLMs
text: Finetuning Existing LLMs
• Gruver et al., finetunes LLaMa-70B to generate CIF files.
• LLMs have highly optimized architecture for leveraging a huge amount of parameters
and can capture complex constraints like charge balance, common oxidation states, etc.

slides.title: Flow-Based Models – FlowMM
text: Flow-Based Models – FlowMM
• Generating the crystal composition and the structure through Riemannian flow matching.

slides.title: MatterGen
text: MatterGen
• State-of-the-art diffusion model for inorganic materials, trained as a foundation model.
• Trained on essentially the entire periodic table (a vast set of materials)
and then can be fine-tuned or guided to many tasks.

slides.title: All-Atom Diffusion Transformer (ADiT)
text: All-Atom Diffusion Transformer (ADiT)
• Training a multi-modal distribution for molecules and materials with latent diffusion.

slides.title: Chemeleon – Text-Guided Crystal Generation
text: Chemeleon – Text-Guided Crystal Generation
• A CLIP-like model that takes natural
language or text descriptions as input
to guide the generation of crystal
structures.

slides.title: Application: Battery
text: Application: Battery
• Charge storage system:
• Cathode: Made of a cathode active material (usually a
lithium metal oxide) that stores lithium ions (Li⁺)
when the battery is discharging.
• Anode: Composed of an anode active material (often
graphite) and enhanced with conductivity-boosting
agents to improve electron flow.
• Discharge process (Powering a Device)
• Lithium ions (Li⁺) move from the anode to the cathode
through the separator (blue porous material).
• Electrons (e⁻) cannot pass through the separator and
instead travel through an external circuit, powering a
device.

slides.title: Application: Battery
text: Application: Battery
• Solid-state electrolytes: A current challenge is to find new crystal compounds that conduct
lithium ions well but are stable and easy to make.
• MatterGen and Chemeleon both explored Li–P–S–Cl quaternary system for Li-ion conductors
Four generated metastable and dynamically
stable materials for Li-P-S-Cl from Chemeleon.

slides.title: Application: Semiconductor
text: Application: Semiconductor
• Semiconductor is a material whose
electrical conductivity lies between that of
conductors and insulators.
• n-type: Doped with donor atoms (e.g.,
Phosphorus) that provide extra electrons.
• p-type: Doped with acceptor atoms (e.g.,
Boron) that create holes (missing electrons).

slides.title: Application: Heterogeneous Catalysis
text: Application: Heterogeneous Catalysis
• Heterogeneous catalysis involves a catalyst in a different phase (usually solid).
• Reactions occur at the surface of the catalyst, where reactant molecules are adsorbed,
transformed, and desorbed as products.
• It is widely used in industry (e.g., catalytic converters, ammonia synthesis, fuel refining)
due to ease of catalyst recovery and reuse.
